sources.headline: They Fled Ethiopia’s War. Now, Israel May Send Them Back.
sources.text:
JERUSALEM—For 75 days starting in 2020, Luwam Habteab slept on the floor of a prison cell, given little food and no medical care. She was detained that November by Ethiopian security forces for her reporting on the Axum massacre, in which Eritrean forces killed hundreds of civilians over a weekend—one of the deadliest episodes of the 2020-22 Tigray war.
Upon her release, Habteab found that her apartment had been sealed by federal police. Her family had warned her not to return there, telling her that security forces were waiting. A local archbishop with a connection at the Israeli Embassy interceded, after which Habteab was ushered out of the country. She landed in Tel Aviv in August 2023 and applied for asylum. (Habteab is identified by a pseudonym out of fear of reprisal.)
Habteab now lives in Jerusalem’s Old City, where she spends most of her days praying. As of August, she was one of 1,334 Ethiopians with open asylum claims before Israel’s Interior Ministry, according to figures that the ministry confirmed to Foreign Policy.
Months after Habteab arrived, in January 2024, the Israeli Interior Ministry determined that the situation in Ethiopia was stable enough to send its nationals home, revoking the group protection that had shielded asylum-seekers from deportation. That stability did not last: This July, Tigray’s regional authorities declared that the 2022 peace agreement with the federal government had collapsed, accusing Addis Ababa of preparing for war.
A multistory residential building featuring open walkways with railings surrounding a central courtyard. In the foreground, laundry hangs from a clothesline, and a profile of a person in a scarf is visible on the right as she passes by the clothes.
A woman walks past clothes left to dry on the balcony of a school used as shelter at a camp for displaced people in Mekelle, in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, on July 19, 2024. Michele Spatari/AFP via Getty Images
Last month, an alliance of rebel groups launched a full-scale offensive against federal forces, seizing airports across Tigray and pushing into neighboring Afar and Amhara states. Federal forces have since retaken Tigray’s capital, though the rebels have vowed to keep fighting; Eritrea and Ethiopia have cut diplomatic ties. Explosions have been reported in Addis Ababa, which Israeli authorities say is safe for returnees.
Habteab has watched with dread as the fighting returned to her home province. Much of Tigray is under a communications blackout, reviving fears of the total siege during the 2020-22 war that starved the region and killed as many as 600,000 people. Habteab’s family in Tigray is almost impossible to reach, she said.
With Israel’s national elections set for Oct. 27, civil society advocates warn that right-wing politicians are once again casting asylum-seekers as a threat to gain a leg up. Israeli officials refer to some migrants and refugees as “infiltrators,” a term embedded in the country’s own laws, and successive governments have described their presence as a danger to Israel’s Jewish character.
Habteab and other asylum-seekers in Israel have few places left to go as domestic politics turn against them and Western governments dismantle the asylum system that was supposed to protect them.
A group of people wearing white garments gather inside a dimly lit stone room. Many hold lit candles, and several individuals hold prayer books or smartphones. Almost everyone has their head covered with either a scarf or a hat.
Ethiopian Orthodox Christian pilgrims light candles during a ceremony on the roof of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem’s Old City on April 19, 2025. John Wessels/AFP via Getty Images
Israel has a long history with the notion of asylum. Founded by refugees in the wake of the Holocaust as a safe haven for the Jewish diaspora, the country was among the first signatories of the 1951 Refugee Convention. Jewish jurists were instrumental in shaping the convention’s core nonrefoulement principle, the rule that no one may be returned to a country where their life is at risk.
Yet, since the Israeli government took over processing asylum claims from the United Nations in 2009, it has granted asylum status to less than 1 percent of those seeking it, according to HIAS Israel, a Jewish humanitarian nonprofit.
Israel has also long held a place in the imagination of Ethiopian asylum-seekers as the land of the ancient Israelites, in whose story of exile and return they saw themselves. In practical terms, the country was also the closest state offering asylum that they could reach without undertaking the perilous Mediterranean crossing.
Of the Ethiopians in Israel who are not Jewish, some—such as Habteab—fled during the Tigray war and its aftermath. But most have been in Israel for a decade or more, arriving on pilgrimage visas or by crossing the Egyptian border before Israel completed its fence there in 2013. They, too, are asylum-seekers: Almost all applied for protection after arriving, having fled earlier rounds of interethnic violence and state persecution, according to the Jerusalem African Community Center (JACC), a support and advocacy organization for the city’s African asylum-seekers.
On arrival, they opened asylum claims with the Interior Ministry and were interviewed about why they had come to Israel. Under Israeli law, the ministry was meant to review each claim and decide whether to grant refugee status—a process that, for most of these asylum-seekers, didn’t happen. Now, according to advocates, many Ethiopian applicants are being summoned back after more than a decade for a second interview to determine whether they can stay in Israel.
An overhead view shows a large crowd of hundreds of people gathered outdoors in an open space. Several national flags are raised above the crowd, including the flags of Israel, Ethiopia, and Eritrea, while speakers stand on a platform with microphones.
Demonstrators wave the former Ethiopian flag, the Eritrean flag, and the Israeli flag as thousands of African asylum-seekers protest against the detention of immigrants and widespread refusal to grant refugee status, seen in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Jan. 5, 2014.Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images
Asked for comment, Israel’s Population and Immigration Authority said, “there is no policy of deportation regarding this group” and that cases are examined individually. The authority added that it does not determine whether a country is safe for returnees, referring questions to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. (The Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.)
Anat Ben-Dor, who runs the Refugee Rights Clinic at Tel Aviv University, said the burden of proof placed on applicants for asylum to establish a credible fear of persecution is set very high and that interviewers look for inconsistencies between what an applicant says now and what they said on arrival.
“The whole interview is actually an effort not to find the truth, but to find flaws and problems in the testimony,” Ben-Dor said. “Very few people can successfully pass such an interview, particularly when the system is so slow that people are being interviewed about events that sometimes occurred 10 years earlier.”
Asked whether the system was dysfunctional or intentionally obstructive, Michal Pomeranz, another lawyer who represents asylum-seekers, said it was both. “They clearly want to make people’s lives here miserable, and that’s something even the Supreme Court has said,” she said, referring to a 2020 ruling that struck down a law requiring asylum-seekers to deposit 20 percent of their wages into a fund that they could recover only by leaving the country.
After the follow-up interview, the Interior Ministry decides whether an asylum-seeker may stay in Israel or must leave—but the outcome is almost always the same, according to Yael Paul Strauss, who runs the psychosocial department at JACC.
By her account, 90 percent to 95 percent of those summoned are rejected and given three to four months to leave the country. “It’s presented as giving them another chance, but in reality, they’re just being called in to be told they have to leave,” Paul Strauss said.
The cost of contesting a rejection is steep, running at around $4,000 to petition a denied application and another $4,000 for an appeal, according to Paul Strauss. Few employers will hire someone with a temporary permit, regardless of their profession or level of education in Ethiopia, leaving most asylum-seekers with few ways to raise that kind of money.
Paul Strauss described a message that she had recently received from a mother of three small children who had paid to appeal her asylum rejection, lost, and had no idea where she would find the money to try again. “She turns to me, ‘Please help me, save my life,’ and I have nothing to give her,” Paul Strauss said.
Two people wearing blue medical scrubs walk away from the camera up steps toward the entrance of a brick building. A blue and white sign planted on the lawn in the foreground reads "VOTE HERE".
A former refugee from Ethiopia (left) arrives to vote for the first time at a polling station in Clarkston, Georgia, in the United States on Nov. 5, 2024. Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP via Getty Images
For many Ethiopian asylum-seekers, the answer to Israel’s stonewalling was to seek resettlement in a third country, another cornerstone of asylum law. For years, the main destination was the United States, which accepted a small number of the most vulnerable cases referred by the U.N. However, that route is now all but closed.
When he returned to office in 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump effectively dismantled the U.S. refugee admissions program and suspended the entry of all refugees into the country, including those who had already been screened. Following legal challenges, the Trump administration resumed limited admissions under a historically low cap of 7,500 refugees for fiscal year 2026—admissions that have been allocated almost entirely to white South African Afrikaners.
In December 2025, the Trump administration also terminated the temporary protected status that Ethiopians were granted during the Tigray war. Around 900 asylum-seekers in Israel—mainly Sudanese and Eritrean, along with some Ethiopians—were in the pipeline to be resettled to the United States as of early 2025, according to Sivan Carmel, the country director of HIAS Israel, which processed the cases.
Some had already cleared their medical and security checks, had departure dates, and needed only plane tickets. “They’d left their jobs; they’d already told their landlords they’d be leaving” before their entry to the United States was denied, Carmel said.
The office of the U.N. refugee agency in Israel, which referred those cases and managed resettlement out of the country, has been hollowed out as part of the same pattern of global retrenchment against asylum—its staff reduced to three and its Tel Aviv office cut. Agency staff struggle to keep up with the thousands of open asylum claims.
This has left the work to fall to groups such as JACC, which operates on a shoestring budget. Paul Strauss spends hours filling in resettlement forms with families who cannot afford a lawyer. Each time Paul Strauss submits a file, she said, the U.N. representative reminds her that completing it does not guarantee placement elsewhere.
For those who cannot leave for another country and cannot stay in Israel, the return of war to Ethiopia has taken away their last consolation: the hope that the danger that they fled might be in the past. As armed forces push toward Ethiopia’s capital and much of Tigray remains in the dark, many of the families that Israel intends to send back can’t even get in touch with their relatives.
For those working on behalf of the asylum-seekers, the bigger picture is not lost. “I want to live in a state that I’m not embarrassed by,” Pomeranz said. “I kept thinking things couldn’t get worse. They keep getting worse.”

sources.headline: Fighting in Ethiopia and the Risk of Regional Spillover
sources.text:
In September, fighting broke out in Ethiopia’s Tigray region between Ethiopian government forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), effectively collapsing the 2022 peace deal. In October, Ethiopian forces recaptured an airport and towns from the TPLF and started moving closer to the border with Eritrea. The renewed conflict raised concerns about both increased instability within Ethiopia — particularly as the TPLF joined with several other armed groups under a new Alliance for Survival — and the potential for a new war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Ethiopia accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF and sending its own forces across the border into Tigray. The two countries severed diplomatic ties.Increased conflict in northern Ethiopia comes amid longstanding regional tensions, including disputes over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam’s impact on the Nile River and landlocked Ethiopia’s ambitions to gain direct access to the sea. We asked five experts to assess the risks that the conflict in Tigray poses for Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia, Sudan, and Egypt.Read more below.William Davison Editor with Africa Confidential Founder of Ethiopia Insight Although unlikely, the biggest risk for Ethiopia is state collapse. This could occur if the TPLF produces stiff resistance that in turn boosts insurgencies in Amhara and Oromia, leading to a rebel march on Addis Ababa — a recipe for worsening disorder.A less dramatic risk is that the federal military gets bogged down in Tigray as the TPLF mounts an insurgency with support from Eritrea. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government would then lose ground against rebels elsewhere. While not an existential threat, this scenario would deepen Ethiopia’s insecurity.The most achievable upside is defeat of the TPLF, the driving force of ethnonationalism. This would mean the failure of the rebel coalition, allowing Abiy to push ahead with constitutional reforms that centralize power and de-ethnicize the federation.If

As U.S. voters head into the final stretch of a high-stakes midterm campaign, President Donald Trump is making his last pitch to a key constituency that has been pummeled by the economic fallout of the Iran war: American farmers.
At a rally in Kansas on Monday, Trump unveiled an $8 billion economic aid package to pacify farmers, who have for months weathered surging diesel and fertilizer prices driven by the war and disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz. The bailout will cover one-time payments for farmers and aims to shield them against market reactions and higher input costs, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).
“When the Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers,” Trump said at the rally for Sen. Roger Marshall, who is up for reelection in Kansas. “We love our farmers.”
By announcing the aid package now, the Trump administration appears to be currying favor with a beleaguered base at a critical moment. But the bailout may be a Band-Aid fix. The Iran war remains the key driver of the global energy crunch, and Trump’s other attempts to drag down diesel prices—including a controversial bid to import Russian diesel—have done little to reassure Americans.
“Unless the underlying problem is resolved, farmers are going to continue to face high costs for diesel,” said Joe Glauber, a former chief economist at the USDA. “This is a temporary thing that is very transparent, and it’s aimed to get voters to vote Republican in November.”
Even as the prices of key commodities have risen in recent months, farmers have faced squeezed margins as the costs of diesel and fertilizer have soared to stubborn highs. It’s not just the disruptions from the Iran war, either. American farmers have also lost valuable market share as a result of Trump’s trade chaos, dating back to the trade war with China during his first term.
As farm bankruptcy filings have risen, so has farm debt, which has more than doubled in the last two decades and is now at a record high of more than $600 billion.
“The challenges farmers face right now are all the bitter fruit of bad policies by the Trump Administration,” Christopher Barrett, an agricultural economist at Cornell University, wrote in an email to Foreign Policy.
All those pressures appear to be taking their toll on the bloc, which has traditionally voted Republican. Polling suggests that frustration with the Trump administration’s policies has grown among farmers. A September survey from Purdue University’s Ag Economy Barometer found that only 48 percent of respondents believed the United States is headed in the “right direction.” In July 2025, when the question was first asked, that figure was 74 percent.
More than half of the survey’s respondents cited higher input costs as a top concern. Respondents were also largely pessimistic about their future financial prospects, with 35 percent saying they expected their operations to be worse off financially one year from now, compared to 22 percent with more positive expectations.
“Farmers are a pretty small population in terms of the overall electorate but in certain races could be very critical,” Glauber said. Longtime red states such as Kansas and Texas, for example, are now seeing highly competitive Senate races, making their states’ rural vote even more decisive.
The $8 billion bailout announcement drew a welcome but somewhat muted response from the American Farm Bureau Federation (AFBF), the country’s biggest general agriculture lobbying group. “We appreciate President Trump and [Agriculture] Secretary [Brooke] Rollins recognizing that higher diesel prices have squeezed farmers’ bottom lines,” AFBF President Zippy Duvall said in a statement.
The aid package only adds to a mountain of financial support offered to farmers by the Trump administration. Even before this bailout was announced, government funding to the agriculture sector was expected to reach about $55 billion in 2026 alone, including an $11 billion funding request still pending approval by Congress. It remains unclear when the latest one-time payments will be delivered.
On average, government payments account for some 30 percent of net farm income right now, Glauber said. Though no one would turn down a check from the federal government, he said, the underlying problems are still unresolved—and no one wants to be too reliant on Uncle Sam.
Farmers would “much rather get a good return from the market and not have to depend on government payments,” Glauber said. “Right now, they are very much dependent.”

sources.headline: The Iran War Has Changed the World Forever
sources.text:
Many of the immediate consequences of the Israeli-American war with Iran are already clear. The further emergence of drones and missiles as dominant weapons of war; the danger to the global economy from the threats to vital chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb; and the inadequacy of U.S. weapons procurement, among other issues, have garnered widespread and entirely merited attention.
Yet as important enough as those developments are, the Iran conflict could also have far wider and longer-term implications—changes that could be truly transformative for the Middle East region and the rest of the world. Decades from now, we might look back on this conflict as a watershed event that fundamentally reshaped what had been bedrock principles of modern geopolitics.
While it would have been better to have discerned these potential break points before the war, there may still be time to take action to try to steer them in favorable directions. As always, the first requirement is to recognize the possible seismic changes that may already be underway.
Gulf States Shifting to Offense—and More War
Aerial satellite footage shows a coastline where a thick plume of black smoke rises from a port area and stretches inland over mountainous terrain.
A satellite view shows a major fire following an Iranian drone strike at the Port of Salalah oil storage tanks in Oman on March 11.Gallo Images/Orbital Horizon/Copernicus Sentinel Data 2026
There has been no shortage of commentary on the new technologies of combat highlighted by the Iran war, with the United States having been mostly focused on defensive systems. Americans have both marveled at the superb performance of Western interceptors and hyperventilated over their dwindling stockpiles of them. However, the Persian Gulf states—and likely many other threatened middle and smaller powers—have taken another lesson from the conflict: The best defense is a good offense.
U.S., Israeli, European, and South Korean interceptor munitions have performed brilliantly, shooting down Iranian ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones. Coupled with the ability of Western fighter aircraft to shoot down drones and cruise missiles—and to suppress the launches of ballistic missiles—Iran has done far less damage to its targets than would otherwise have been the case. In short, air and missile defenses have performed extremely well so far. That’s not nothing.
The problem is that it has not proved to be anything close to enough. Because drones; cruise missiles; and even, to a considerable extent, ballistic missiles are so much cheaper, easier to produce, store, hide, and launch than most of the interceptors that the United States and its allies use against them, Iran has been able to keep making more and launching them at targets across the Gulf, Jordan, and Israel. Even though the defenses are stopping roughly 90 percent of them, the 10 percent that are getting through are 100 percent too many.
Only the Israeli population is inured enough and its infrastructure hardened enough to prove undaunted by Iran’s counterstrikes. In stark contrast, the same levels of damage have proved catastrophic for the Gulf states. Energy companies, shipping companies, and insurance companies are all balking at the prospect of functioning with the residual threat of constant Iranian attacks, even if more than 90 percent are defeated. The 10 percent that have gotten through have done significant physical damage and far greater psychological damage. They called into question the current and planned future socioeconomic model of the Gulf states.
All of the modern Gulf economies were built in the expectation that their lands would be peaceful havens for commerce, hydrocarbon production, rest, and relaxation. Iran’s drone and missile attacks have shattered that, undermining the energy, manufacturing, trade, finance, investment, and tourism industries of the Gulf.
Who is going to want to invest, manufacture, or vacation in countries that are periodically subject to missile and drone attacks, even if nearly all of them are intercepted? Who wants to conduct business, import oil, invest money, trade goods, or take a vacation in a place where, a few times a week (or day), you hear explosions overhead, even if they are the sound of defensive systems successfully intercepting attacking munitions?
At some level, the Gulf governments understood this. However, what they assumed before the war was that the threat of massive retaliation by the United States (or Israel, after the Abraham Accords), would limit the size and scope of Iranian missile and drone attacks—enabling their defenses to defeat any small retaliations that Tehran thought necessary for honor’s sake.
They were counting on the restraint that Iran had consistently shown in the past, including as recently as the short June 2025 war, because Iran had always feared that a larger response would trigger a U.S. bid for regime change.
Of course, in this war, by trying—and failing—to achieve regime change and then taking it off the table altogether, the United States has turned that logic on its head. Iran now has the ability to threaten both the Gulf economies directly with missile and drone attacks and the global economy by throttling tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz without fear of a U.S. effort to overthrow its regime. Americans know that they can’t achieve regime change by air power alone and (so far) lack the political will to employ the ground forces that would be necessary to do it for certain. With the threat of regime change gone, it is Iran that has demonstrated that it can deter U.S. and Israeli attacks at least as effectively as the United States and Israel can limit Iranian attacks on the Gulf.
This state of affairs—in which the Gulf states now have such reservations about relying on the United States (or Israel) to deter Iranian attack—is intolerable. It is why they are all purchasing or contemplating acquiring fleets of drones and missiles of their own. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Kuwait are all purchasing Turkish drones, while the Saudis are working with U.S. corporations to begin to build thousands of their own. Likewise, the UAE is trying to acquire drones and drone manufacturing capabilities from Israel, China, and Ukraine. Qatar and Bahrain are in talks to do the same.
A top-down aerial view shows two large grey uncrewed aircraft with long wings parked one right in front of the other on an asphalt tarmac.
Bayraktar AKINCI unmanned aerial vehicles in Elazig, Turkey, on Sept. 23.Bestami Bodruk/Anadolu via Getty Images
While it could prove that a balance of terror will impose a wary peace on drone- and missile-armed adversaries on both sides of the Gulf, just as the Cold War did for the United States and Soviet Union, that outcome is much less likely in this instance. As Bernard Brodie famously said back in 1946, what made a nuclear balance so effective at keeping the pace was the unmistakable power of nuclear weapons. No one could misunderstand what would happen if even a single nuclear weapon—let alone several dozen—were detonated in their country. When both the Gulf states and Iran possess thousands of conventional drones and missiles, that certainty of incalculable damage will be absent.
Instead, the arsenals will probably serve as a spur to further warfare. Iran will see the Gulf states attempting to build offensive strike forces of their own and will want to demonstrate that these will not be enough to deter Iranian attacks. The hard-line fanatics now in charge in Tehran will want to ensure that the conservative Gulf monarchs believe that Iran can take far more punishment than they can, and so Iran will look for opportunities to strike the Gulf to prove it.
In turn, the Gulf states will feel the need to retaliate to establish that they won’t be bullied and can give as good as they get. And the United States may well choose to keep out for fear that coming to the defense of the Gulf states will cause Iran to shut down the Strait of Hormuz again. All of this portends multiple missile and drone exchanges as each side seeks to bolster its capabilities, find weaknesses in the other side to exploit, and demonstrate its resolve.
As bad as this is likely to be, there is one more unfortunate development to consider. Once the Gulf states acquire the capacity to project power beyond their borders—something that none of them has had for roughly a century—they are likely to start using it and using it to do things that the United States won’t necessarily like.
This, too, has been the history of the Gulf. In the 1970s, when the United States armed the Iranian shah in hope that he would relieve some of Washington’s defense burden in the region, he began using his new military to do all kinds of things that the United States did not like, from backing the Kurds against Saddam Hussein to seizing Gulf islands from the UAE. Likewise, over the past decade, at American urging, the UAE has developed modest power projection capabilities of its own, which it has been using to pursue its interests in Yemen, Libya, Sudan, and the Horn of Africa, often in opposition to U.S. policies.
The Gulf is acquiring offensive military capabilities for the first time in modern history. We can call it burden-sharing, and perhaps it will mean that the United States will no longer have to defend them and their invaluable energy exports. But it seems far more likely to provoke greater conflict in the region, and to convince other states in other parts of the world that they should and can do the same.
China Beginning to Project Power
A large cargo ship traveling across open water, its deck fully loaded with rows of white semi-truck cabs.
A cargo ship carrying Chinese trucks for export to Middle Eastern countries sails in the waters of Yantai, Shandong province, China, on July 20. Costfoto/NurPhoto via Getty Images
For roughly the past four decades, China has been the ultimate free rider in the Middle East. Beijing has relied on Washington to keep the region stable by dealing with its endless security problems—from interstate wars to intrastate wars—and allow China to concentrate on enriching itself through favorable trade, investment, and infrastructure construction.
In their defense, the Chinese haven’t been subtle or bashful about it. I once had the Chinese vice minister for foreign affairs berate me for the United States’ failure to keep the peace of the region on China’s behalf. He literally shouted at me that China did not understand the Middle East, with its religion and “craziness,” and so it was Washington’s responsibility to keep things quiet—a responsibility that he felt Americans were failing at. I wasn’t even in the U.S. government at the time.
Moreover, the Chinese certainly weren’t the first, even if they may have been the most blatant. For almost a century, the United States played China to Britain’s United States. Beginning in the 19th century, American merchants plied the waters of the Gulf in search of lucre, deliberately disdainful of local politics and conflict, leaving all of that to the British until London withdrew its forces from the region in the early 1970s. Even then, the United States did not fully take on the role of regional hegemon until the 1990s, after the Iranian revolution, the Iran-Iraq War, and Saddam’s invasion of Kuwait convinced Washington that the region would not remain stable on its own.
So, like the United States—and even to a lesser extent, Britain—before it, China has been allowed to ignore the constant problems of the Gulf by leaving them to someone else. However, the events of the past decade, more so the past three years, and even more so the past six months, have been calling the viability of this arrangement into question.

sources.headline: Tehran is a Different Beast Now
sources.text: The Tehran that the world knew is gone. It died in the fires with former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on the first day of the war in February. His son and new Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei — wherever he is and in whatever physical condition — witnessed his father, wife, and other close family members die in the same airstrike that wounded him. The White House believed that the conflict would last only a few weeks, but the Islamic Republic has proven less fragile than anticipated by the United States and Israel, who now must deal with surviving Iranian leaders who experienced similar trauma and loss in early strikes. Washington has struggled to appreciate how its devastating attacks altered Tehran’s mindset: The White House instead still expresses confusion at “crazy” Iranian behavior that won’t return to prewar expectations.I argue here that the “crazy” Iranian behavior confounding Washington in part reflects a subtle but important shift in Iran’s mindset. The U.S.-led attack was end-of-days fodder for true believers inside the upper echelons of the Islamic Republic, who listened to years of paranoid predictions about just such an apocalyptic attack at weekly Friday prayers. The surviving members of Iran’s inner circle — the New Tehran — are now acting based on an altered set of strategic principles. Despite the tactical brilliance of the U.S. military, the White House cannot find an endgame and risks turning a crisis into a catastrophe if it cannot adjust to Tehran’s new reality.As a former CIA analyst, my job for many years was to set aside my personal views and instead see the world as Iranian leaders do. My goal was to get inside the heads of Tehran’s hardliners, who have very different perspectives than Western analysts. Such an exercise can be uncomfortable to do with violent authoritarians hostile to the United States — especially when the exercise challenges one’s core assumptions and values — but it provides helpful clarity when an adversary’s behavior defies expectations. Of course, Iranian leaders do not regularly broadcast their private deliberations — and their public statements can be misleading bravado and propaganda. So divining Iran’s true leadership decision-making is often more art than science. Yet, it is still possible to deduce much of their unspoken internal logic by analyzing regime actions and viewing the world through Tehran’s ideological lens.The White House is engaged in an intense game of Kremlinology, seeking to figure out which leaders are up and down in Tehran. Iran’s decimated inner circle faces internal divisions, which almost certainly are compounded by the uncertainty of Mojtaba Khamenei’s status. Some Western observers have characterized the regime’s condition as leaderless anger incapable of making peace. However, the simplest explanation is that U.S.-Israeli decapitation strikes shifted Iran’s political center of gravity towards the military hardliners around Mojtaba Khamenei who are responsible for fighting the war and who favor more aggressive tactics without Ali Khamenei’s natural caution as a buffer. Public squabbling and factional rivalries are a hallmark of politics in the Islamic Republic, but are often over-indexed by Western observers, so hope that some internal regime fissure will ease America’s dilemma is unrealistic. If the regime survives a few more years, differences between Iran’s newly shuffled leaders perhaps could widen into gulfs and present real forks in the road for Iran, but a shared bunker mentality during this crisis almost certainly will keep their tactical disagreements from being too meaningful for U.S. policy.Right now, too much focus on Tehran’s leadership dynamics is a distraction that prevents Washington from stepping back and acknowledging that there is some broad strategic coherence to New Tehran’s harder-line posture. Taken collectively, Iran’s actions in the past seven months can be read as reflecting a sober reassessment based on its bitter lessons from the war. New Tehran recognizes that there is little to gain by playing it safe: Its only chance to survive is an aggressive posture that imposes enough cost that the United States and its regional partners can no longer easily threaten the Islamic Republic’s existence — even if that brinksmanship brings the regime’s own survival to the edge.Below are key elements of New Tehran’s mindset. Understanding how they affect Iranian behavior will be critical for Washington to recalibrate its assumptions and successfully conclude the war.Can’t Deter “Dead Men Walking.”The unprecedented decapitation strikes on Iran’s leadership have likely persuaded its surviving members that they are “dead men walking.” The regime change rhetoric from hawks in the United States and Israel during successive attacks on Iran probably has convinced Tehran that its enemies will never stop trying to “finish the job” until the regime and its leadership cadre are dead, regardless of whether there is a ceasefire to end this current round of conflict. President Donald Trump’s regular threats to annihilate the regime probably keep their personal survival top of mind. The question for regime leaders is probably whether the United States and Israel will try again to kill them next month or next year. Iranian leaders likely see more decapitation strikes after the U.S. midterm elections as a credible threat, given reporting that the White House is considering more attacks. Indeed, Mojtaba Khamenei’s disappearing act can probably be explained by the regime’s fear of another targeted attack if the United States and Israel could ever confirm his location.In 2019, Iran accepted an off-ramp to the conflict started after the United States killed Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps – Qods Force Commander Qassem Soleimani. Ali Khamenei feared that all-out war would risk regime survival and encouraged “strategic patience.” Last summer, Iran again accepted a ceasefire to conclude the “12-day war” after Israel and the United States struck Iranian military and nuclear facilities. Ali Khamenei again feared escalation and accepted another ceasefire. More than likely, Iran’s hardliners have since privately concluded that Ali Khamenei’s decision to play it safe ultimately cost him his life.While this “dead men walking” mindset has eroded U.S. and Israeli deterrence, Iranian leaders are not suicidal and would prefer to find a way to secure their country’s future with their lives intact. Yet, like those committed to ideologies and nationalities around the world, they will die in defense of the Islamic Republic if necessary. And like leaders in many countries, they will maximize the pain for their enemies before their demise.Iran’s leaders also likely view their survival after the massive U.S.-Israeli bombing campaign as demonstrating the limits of air power alone. Tehran has grown accustomed to Trump’s threats of massive escalation. But Iran’s inner circle probably asks itself: What is he going to do that Iran has not already endured? Will he kill the Supreme Leader again? Pile more rubble on Iran’s nuclear facilities? He has already done all of these things — and continues to conduct periodic airstrikes on Iran’s military to “mow the lawn.” A red line Trump has threatened to cross but largely held back is bombing Iran’s civilian infrastructure, such as water and electricity. Iran has warned that it will inflict the same pain back onto Gulf Arab civilian infrastructure — which is more vulnerable to failure, hence the Gulf’s private pleadings with Trump to avoid such escalation. Iran is mindful that the United States still could send in ground troops and force regime change as it did with Saddam Hussein’s Iraq. However, the regime knows how unlikely such a deeply unpopular step would be for the White House, especially given its belief that many of its 90 million citizens would help turn its territory into another quagmire for the U.S. military.The Israeli Threat is Endemic, The U.S. Threat is ExistentialWhile Iranian leaders recognize that the United States has the military heft to end the Islamic Republic — even if Tehran is skeptical that Trump is willing to pay the high price necessary to do so — Tehran probably calculates that Israel’s small but sophisticated conventional military lacks the mass alone to bring down the Islamic Republic. Which is probably why, in Tehran’s likely estimation, Israeli leaders spent so much energy convincing the United States to join attacks on Iran and accomplish what Israel could not. Iranian leaders almost certainly have watched the gap widen between American and Israeli goals as the war dragged on, with Israel annoyed that the United States doesn’t seem as committed to regime change. Iran expects its deadly battles with Israel across the region to continue — and Iran understands just how lethal Israel can be — but Iranian eyes remain focused on the unique existential threat posed by the U.S. role in the war.Facts on the Ground, Not Cheap TalkThe United States has sent repeated diplomatic feelers to Iranian leaders through various creative channels about ending the conflict, but Iran’s constant rebuffs indicate that they see most U.S. diplomatic offers as cups of poison. Many Iranian leaders are wary that the United States and Israel launched surprise attacks on Iran twice in the past two years when Tehran’s diplomats were in negotiations with Washington. This pattern probably has confirmed Iranian hardliners’ cynicism that the White House often uses negotiations as a military tactic — either for misdirection to lull Iranian defenses or as a pause to allow the U.S. military time for rest and reinforcements before coming back once more to finish the job. In June, Tehran almost certainly was willing to try the short-lived Memorandum of Understanding because it was sequenced in a way to test whether Washington was indeed willing to accept changed facts on the ground. From Iran’s perspective, the agreement was more than just a simple de-escalatory off-ramp because it recognized Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz — administered jointly with Oman — as a security guarantee against future U.S. attack. It also provided significant sanctions relief without offering any concrete concessions in Iran’s nuclear program. Iranians allege that the United States immediately set about skirting its obligations, including undermining Iranian control of the strait, which Tehran saw as just further evidence of American duplicity.No Urgency to End Hormuz StandoffTrump was reportedly surprised that Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz. The irony is that Iran had not previously closed the strait because it feared U.S. military reprisal for doing so. But once Iran had already suffered the very attack it feared, that calculus flipped. If Tehran had ever attempted to close the strait preemptively, Washington would have been able to organize a worldwide coalition against Iran’s aggression. But because the United States initiated this round of conflict without consulting allies, Europe and Asia will not join a U.S. coalition to help Washington out of its strategic predicament. The U.S.-Israeli attack gave Iran a path to finally wield the strait as a geographic cudgel, and New Tehran is keen to make Washington taste its own medicine: economic pain.The U.S. military has performed impressive work since August: clawing back open lanes in the strait by escorting tankers, clearing mines, destroying Iran’s closest launch sites, and blinding Iran’s radar systems, briefly almost reaching pre-war shipping levels in late September. Iran’s leaders almost certainly view this partial opening as a tactical development that can be reversed with perseverance and escalation. sources.headline: UK fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
sources.text:
Britain will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom against increasing attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, the UK government announced on Tuesday.
The aircraft will protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from drones and missiles, the Ministry of Defense said. They will not carry out offensive strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.
"The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable," British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said.
He particularly condemned attacks on Riyadh's international airport, which has been targeted 20 times since the beginning of October.
Strikes on the airport have killed at least 18 people and wounded hundreds this month, according to reports.UK sends warplanes as Saudi Arabia seeks more help against HouthisTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
What additional military support is Britain providing?
The deployment follows a request from Saudi Arabia and expands military assistance announced by London in September.Britain will also send an Atlas A400M military transport aircraft and military advisers. It has extended its offer to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi aircraft operating against the Houthis for another 90 days.
The announcement comes as Yemen's civil war continues to escalate following the collapse of a years-long truce in September.
Houthi attacks have increasingly targeted Saudi oil facilities and civilian infrastructure. The rebels have also imposed a naval blockade and attacked tankers, disrupting oil exports and pushing up energy prices.
Inside Yemen, authorities said a Houthi strike on Monday killed 58 people at a training camp for Saudi-backed government security forces.
Saudi Arabia and the United States accuse Iran of supporting the Houthis, an allegation Tehran denies.Riyadh's international airport has seen a string of attacks claimed by the HouthisImage: Social Media/REUTERS
How is the conflict affecting Saudi Arabia's economy?
Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, informally known as "Davos in the Desert," until 2027.
The event, originally scheduled for October 26-29, was expected to attract leading international financiers.
According to media reports, major banks and private equity firms had raised security concerns about attending the event.
The conference is a key part of Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract foreign investment and diversify its economy away from oil.

sources.headline: Witkoff Pushes Putin to Restart Peace Talks
sources.text:
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff courting Russian President Vladimir Putin, the United Kingdom’s approval of an offshore natural gas project, and psychological warfare on the Korean Peninsula.
Witkoff Courts Putin in St. Petersburg
Less than 24 hours after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff held high-stakes talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway, U.S. President Donald Trump’s go-to negotiator flew to Russia for an ambitious meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday. The focus: restarting Ukraine peace talks.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff courting Russian President Vladimir Putin, the United Kingdom’s approval of an offshore natural gas project, and psychological warfare on the Korean Peninsula.
Witkoff Courts Putin in St. Petersburg
Less than 24 hours after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff held high-stakes talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway, U.S. President Donald Trump’s go-to negotiator flew to Russia for an ambitious meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday. The focus: restarting Ukraine peace talks.
In recent weeks, Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with the continuation of the war in Ukraine, especially as high fuel prices at home risk undermining the Republican Party’s performance in next month’s midterm elections. Trump’s ire, however, has primarily centered on Kyiv—not Moscow.
Last week, Ukraine accused the Trump administration of abruptly limiting its access to military-grade Starlink satellite services and of threatening to withhold information crucial to its defense. Trump had repeatedly urged Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, even as Moscow continued to target Kyiv’s power grid.
Meanwhile, the White House suspended U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports last week and floated a multibillion-dollar deal with Russia’s Lukoil.
Even though Trump has argued that Ukraine should find “somebody else ​to negotiate” other than Zelensky, the White House has expressed no such qualms with Putin. Instead, Witkoff appeared to pull out all the stops to curry favor with the Kremlin on Wednesday, including by stroking Putin’s ego.
“You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again,” Witkoff told Putin, who is wanted as a war criminal by the International Criminal Court. The comments were made after Moscow released a U.S. citizen detained in Russia since 2022 as part of a goodwill gesture.
The flattery may have worked. Russia confirmed on Wednesday that Putin has agreed to resume U.S.-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month. The negotiations are likely to be on the technical level, such as how to ensure Ukraine’s security once the conflict ends.
However, Moscow did not give any indication that it is willing to compromise on some of its biggest demands, including full Russian control of the occupied Donetsk region, a halt to Ukraine’s NATO membership ambitions, and the establishment of a peace deal without first securing a cease-fire.
“Russia would like to get it done,” Trump said on Tuesday, referring to reaching a peace agreement. However, he expressed doubt that Zelensky wants to end the conflict. “If they don’t make a deal, it’s just going to get worse” for Ukraine, he added.
Zelensky responded with his own caveats, reiterating calls for a cease-fire while agreeing to freeze his military’s front line. At the same time, Ukraine carried out more strikes on Russian energy infrastructure on Wednesday, doubling down on a pledge to target such sites so long as Russia continues to do so.
Still, the Trump administration is painting Witkoff’s back-to-back meetings as “constructive,” especially as Putin appears eager to foster closer ties with the United States.

The Iran War Has Changed the World Forever by Kenneth M. Pollack
How Ukraine Is Navigating Trump’s Latest U-Turn by Keith Johnson
What We’re Following
Drill, baby, drill. The British government approved a controversial offshore natural gas project in the North Sea on Wednesday, silencing dissent from activists who denounced the continued extraction of fossil fuels. The United Kingdom has characterized the deal as a “pragmatic” approach to improve its energy security as global fuel prices skyrocket.
“But even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come,” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement on Wednesday while also pledging billions of dollars to a new fund focused on expanding the country’s renewable energy development.
Britain hopes that Jackdaw field, located off the coast of Scotland, will reduce its reliance on imported fuel and make households less susceptible to price volatility. Another winner of the gas deal, though, is Trump, who has long pressured the U.K. to “open up” the North Sea to new drilling projects.
Trump applauded the decision on Truth Social, calling the North Sea “one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of OIL in the World” and arguing that the U.K. “should go FULL BLAST!!!”
Loudspeaker warfare in the DMZ. North Korea has announced that it will activate propaganda speakers along its entire border with South Korea by the end of October. According to Kim Yo Jong, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s sister, tactical teams will also take up new positions along the demilitarized zone to provide support for Pyongyang’s “psychological warfare” operation against Seoul.
North Korea also warned its troops on Wednesday to take “prompt ​and resolute action” if South Korean forces threaten their safety. Animosity between the countries has worsened in recent years, particularly after North Korea fortified its border in April 2024. Pyongyang and Seoul have since used psychological warfare tactics, from speakers blaring K-pop songs to balloons filled with trash and excrement.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has made easing tensions on the peninsula a centerpiece of his foreign-policy platform. But that hasn’t stopped Seoul from accusing North Korean troops of crossing the demarcation line at least 50 times this year or from vowing on Tuesday to “resolutely” punish any further North Korean provocations.
Carney seeking new partners. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney traveled to Turkey on Wednesday to bolster ties in energy, defense, and trade cooperation. He will be the first Canadian head of government to visit Ankara for a dedicated bilateral trip, after which he will meet with Turkish business leaders in Istanbul.
The historic visit is part of Carney’s efforts to decrease economic dependence on the United States in the face of sweeping U.S. tariffs. Nuclear energy will likely be at the top of Carney’s agenda with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Over the summer, both countries’ trade ministers identified areas of collaboration involving Canada’s CANDU nuclear reactor technology. Ottawa is looking to expand its nuclear energy partnerships to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels, while Ankara is hoping to use CANDU to build its own nuclear plant on the Black Sea coast.
Joint cooperation is also expected to focus on defense procurement, specifically concerning the production of ammunition, drones, and counter-drone weaponry. Turkey is one of the world’s leading defense exporters, with sales surpassing $11 billion in 2025. Canada has tried to bolster its defense investments to meet NATO’s minimum spending pledge.
Odds and Ends
Everyone has pet peeves. For FP’s World Brief writer, it’s when kitchen drawers are left cracked open. For Britain’s Burnham, it’s when people riding buses or trains listen to music or videos without headphones.
On Monday, Burnham announced a nationwide campaign against what he called “one of the most annoying things on public transport,” encouraging local leaders to crack down on “nuisance” behaviors by fining passengers or asking them to leave. Now, if only Burnham could promote a ban on unkempt cooking areas.

sources.headline: Zelensky Seeks U.S. Support, but Is Trump Interested?
sources.text:
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Ukraine’s deteriorating relationship with the United States, government measures to tackle protests across Europe, and the Houthis’ deadliest strike in Yemen since fighting resumed in July.
Zelensky Meets Witkoff in Oslo
As U.S. President Donald Trump looks increasingly interested in currying favor with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky hopes that a face-to-face with White House special envoy Steve Witkoff will be enough to repair ties before the U.S. president throws more support behind Moscow.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Ukraine’s deteriorating relationship with the United States, government measures to tackle protests across Europe, and the Houthis’ deadliest strike in Yemen since fighting resumed in July.
Zelensky Meets Witkoff in Oslo
As U.S. President Donald Trump looks increasingly interested in currying favor with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky hopes that a face-to-face with White House special envoy Steve Witkoff will be enough to repair ties before the U.S. president throws more support behind Moscow.
Zelensky flew to Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday to attend a slew of meetings focused on Russia’s war in Ukraine and European security. They included talks with Witkoff—and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, who attended virtually—that touched on allegations of Washington withholding critical intelligence from Kyiv as well as Zelensky’s efforts to get more U.S.-made Patriot missiles.
Last week, Ukraine abruptly lost access to military-grade Starlink satellite services, disrupting several missions. Kyiv and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk accused the Trump administration of ordering the cuts; Trump denied doing so. That, coupled with reports that U.S. military officials had threatened to restrict intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, pushed Zelensky to scrap a Trump-declared truce on energy strikes between Russia and Ukraine.
That move appeared to frustrate the White House. On Monday, Trump said that “Russia, frankly, has been fine ​on Ukraine,” that “Zelensky is not helping matters much,” and that Ukraine should find “somebody else ​to negotiate.” He also suggested that the United States is open to talks with Russia and China on the future of Ukraine, worrying European allies that they will be left out.
Trump has recently tried to bring down fuel prices by pressuring Ukraine to give in to Russia’s demands. That included suspending U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports, which a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers called “a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies,” and a possible multibillion-dollar deal with Russia’s Lukoil (as well as the short-lived truce on energy strikes).
Zelensky initially called the diesel deal a “happy birthday” present for Russian President Vladimir Putin and told the Financial Times last week that Trump has an affinity for dictators. But on Tuesday, Zelensky appeared to change his tune, instead writing on X that Ukraine is “grateful” for continued U.S. support.
Still, Zelensky didn’t fully bend to Trump’s demands. Following his talks with Witkoff and Kushner, Zelensky offered to halt strikes on Russian energy again—but only if Moscow does so as well. Less than 24 hours earlier, Russian forces launched new ballistic missile and jet-powered drone strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Zelensky said that Kyiv did not receive any advance warning of the attack, a nod to the country’s deteriorating ties with Washington and its inadequate supply of Patriot missiles.
Today’s Most Read
The Iran War Has Changed the World Forever by Kenneth M. Pollack
Why Is France Perpetually Rioting? by Emile Chabal
An Underwater Shadow War Is Raging by John Kampfner
What We’re Following
Europe’s season of protest. Several French cities extended their curfews through Tuesday after Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu argued that they were “efficient” at quelling widespread unrest. “They helped to restore calm last night,” Lecornu said, vowing to deploy a massive security force ahead of planned demonstrations on Saturday, dubbed “Act II.”
Weeks of anti-government protests over inadequate public services and the rising cost of living transformed over the weekend into one of the country’s worst bouts of rioting in decades. Security personnel arrested more than 2,400 demonstrators, and clashes injured hundreds of police officers.
Experts say the unrest is feeding similar protest movements across Europe, including Spain’s housing reform sit-ins, Albania’s anti-corruption demonstrations, and Belgium’s education reform push. That also includes Italy’s cost-of-living crisis, which this week saw some protesters resort to similar acts of looting and vandalism in Milan.
On Tuesday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced that she will send 500 troops to the city to help restore calm. Her government also pledged to approve new security measures in the coming days, such as extending preventive detentions for minors, banning gatherings for people considered a threat to public order, and cracking down on youth gangs.
Deadly Houthi attacks. Houthi rebels launched a devastating ballistic missile strike on a Yemeni military camp on Monday, killing at least 73 people—all new recruits between ages 18 and 20. Monday’s assault was the deadliest strike in the country since Houthi forces restarted fighting in July after a nearly four-year cease-fire.
On Tuesday, the Iranian-backed group launched missile and drone attacks across Saudi Arabia as well as on the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz—part of a monthslong offensive intended to secure control of the strategic Red Sea coast. Such attacks have pushed Riyadh close to its breaking point, prompting the country to implement unorthodox measures to counter the rebel group.
Saudi Arabia this month triggered a mutual defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey; the latter submitted the deal to parliament for ratification on Tuesday. The United Kingdom has announced that it will deploy fighter jets to Saudi Arabia to help defend against Houthi drones. And the Egyptian Parliament is expected to vote next week on whether to authorize its own military support.
But foreign support is unlikely to help Saudi Arabia bear the immediate economic fallout of Houthi attacks. On Monday, the kingdom postponed its annual Future Investment Initiative, originally scheduled for next week, in the wake of several deadly strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
Analysts argue that canceling “Davos in the Desert” will hinder Saudi Arabia’s efforts to make its economy less dependent on oil and natural gas profits.
Alberta votes to remain. Alberta residents voted on Monday to remain part of Canada in the resource-rich province’s first separatist referendum. According to results announced on Tuesday, around 76 percent of Albertans rejected independence, delivering a major political victory to Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Carney has sought to promote a common Canadian identity to help oppose sweeping U.S. tariffs and other threats from the White House. “Albertans made a clear choice,” Carney said on Tuesday. “They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other.”
Carney previously warned Albertans that voting to leave Canada would be “a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division.” Still, this likely isn’t the end of the province’s quest for independence; 62 percent of locals believe that “there will never ⁠be an ​end to the separatist movement,” according to data from Angus Reid Institute pollsters released on Friday.
The nonbinding referendum’s failure also does not signal the end of Carney’s internal dissent challenges. The pro-separatist Parti Québécois narrowly won a provincial election this month, after which it vowed to hold its own independence referendum in Quebec once Trump leaves office.
Odds and Ends
UNESCO recognized Austria’s Wurstelprater amusement park in Vienna as an “immaterial cultural heritage” site on Saturday. Established in 1895, the open-air funfair is one of the oldest amusement parks in the world. However, its significance to the country dates back even further to when the grounds were used as an aristocratic hunting site starting in the 12th century.
Nowadays, Wurstelprater is free to enter and remains open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. So, there is plenty of time to ride the Black Mamba, sit atop its famous Giant Ferris Wheel, or visit the Prater Museum.

sources.headline: How Ukraine Is Navigating Trump’s Latest U-Turn
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he would be open to talks with Russia and China over the future of Ukraine, arguing that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much.” That came amid an onslaught of Russian drone and ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian hospitals, schools, and energy facilities.
The reason that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is pleading for a complete restoration of Starshield, the military internet service provided by SpaceX, along with full intelligence sharing with Washington and the delivery of Patriot missiles, is precisely because of the stepped-up pace of Moscow’s aerial offensive.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he would be open to talks with Russia and China over the future of Ukraine, arguing that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much.” That came amid an onslaught of Russian drone and ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian hospitals, schools, and energy facilities.
The reason that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is pleading for a complete restoration of Starshield, the military internet service provided by SpaceX, along with full intelligence sharing with Washington and the delivery of Patriot missiles, is precisely because of the stepped-up pace of Moscow’s aerial offensive.
Just in September, Moscow launched almost 4,000 attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine—a 65 percent increase over the year before—with 145 strikes damaging Ukrainian energy infrastructure, according to the Kyiv School of Economics. The attacks are especially deadly for civilians, with more than 300 killed last month, an 85 percent increase over the year before, and the pace is only intensifying in the first half of October, the United Nations monitoring mission in Ukraine said.
The Russian drone-and-missile offensive is meant, like each one before it in every winter of the war, to leave Ukrainians in the dark and cold during winter, in a bid to break popular support for continuing to fight. Moscow launched 76 attacks on energy targets in just the past week. Zelensky said on Monday that the attacks continued over the weekend in about a dozen regions and warned that combined-heat-and-power plants, critical for heating during winter, remain vulnerable.
In response, Ukraine itself this year has greatly stepped up its own aerial offensive, especially against Russian oil facilities—precisely the reason Trump soured on Zelensky at a time of sky-high gas and diesel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections. But the Ukrainian long-range strikes, coupled with years of Western sanctions, have successfully choked off much of Moscow’s energy earnings, the life blood of its war machine. The Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries—the direct cause of Trump’s ire—have been especially effective, with Russian exports of refined products at their second-lowest level of the war last month.
Zelensky met with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday for another round of talks, with Jared Kushner joining remotely. The Ukrainian president reiterated his willingness to accept a mutual cease-fire on attacks on energy facilities but only if Moscow reciprocates.
The pressing concern for Ukraine this fall is that the Russian strikes threaten to overwhelm an energy system that has been battered but has still survived four winters of war. Not a day has gone by since mid-July without a Russian attack on Ukrainian energy facilities, Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said over the weekend, with more than 2,000 strikes during that time. Ukraine has now lost about two-thirds of its prewar electricity generation capacity.
Both Ukraine’s power sector and Russian attack capabilities have evolved during the war. Ukrainian power plants have been hardened, with protective shielding and more robust air defenses, and the electricity system itself has been made more resilient through decentralization, including a greater use of renewable energy. Russian attacks, though, have kept pace with Ukraine’s efforts; the introduction of jet-powered drones, coupled with long-range ballistic missiles, is making it harder for Ukraine to prevent the increasing number of successful Russian strikes.
That’s why the sudden reversal of U.S. policy this month—including limitations on Ukraine’s use of Starshield, lingering questions over U.S. intelligence sharing (such as warnings of ballistic missile launches), and a U.S. refusal so far to allow European partners to transfer Patriot interceptors to Ukraine—has caused Zelensky so much concern.
Almost all regions of the country have been damaged by Russian strikes, said Slawomir Matuszak, an expert on the Ukrainian economy at the Centre for Eastern Studies in Warsaw, Poland. But he said the nationwide electricity crisis is not notably worse than in prior years. The real problem, he said, is in Kyiv, which even in the best of times doesn’t generate all its own electricity and relies on imports from other regions. Now, all three of Kyiv’s power plants have been taken offline, and Russia has systematically switched its targeting to destroy high-voltage transmission, said Ukrenergo, the country’s transmission system operator.
“I’d go as far as to say that, at the national level, the situation isn’t any worse than it was a year ago,” Matuszak said. “However, things are much more difficult in Kyiv, as almost all power generation capacity within the city was destroyed in January and February, meaning that nearly all the electricity now has to be supplied from outside the city.”
Zelensky said on Monday that more than half a million people were without power after Moscow’s weekend attacks. On Tuesday, Russia again struck a substation in the capital, knocking out power across Kyiv and paralyzing public transport.
The transmission strikes also make it harder for Europe to provide assistance to Ukraine, Matuszak said. Even though Europe can supply more than 2 gigawatts of electricity to Ukraine, the damaged transmission network makes it hard to send that power to needy regions, especially in the capital and cities farther east. And that is a particular challenge, the grid operator said, because Russian strikes often target repair crews trying to fix the damage from previous attacks.

sources.text:
Welcome to The Ukraine Compass, a weekly digest of Ukrainian commentary and analysis from across the political spectrum only for War on the Rocks members. Each week, we bring you a curated selection of articles from Ukrainian media offering insight into how Ukrainians themselves debate the issues shaping their country.Western coverage often narrows the view to the battlefield — these pieces widen it, revealing the texture of daily life, politics, and public argument in a nation at war. The perspectives gathered here are varied, candid, and often surprising, together forming a more complete picture of Ukraine as it really is.Frontline and StrategyУкраїнська правда — Ukrainska Pravda (“Ukrainian Truth”)Highly influential centrist-liberal outlet with a strongly pro-reform voice“It’s Time to Explain the Plan for Ending the War”By Yuriy Lutsenko/Oct. 14, 2026Yuriy Lutsenko argues President Trump has betrayed Ukraine by lifting the ban on Russian diesel trade during escalating Russian strikes on civilians, abandoning the principle of not easing pressure on the aggressor before a ceasefire. He claims the move serves Trump family business interests pursued by Witkoff and Kushner, won’t lower prices as he claims, and has been accompanied by disruptions to early-warning intelligence and Starlink-equipped drones. He also blames President Zelensky’s governance and urges major fixes to end the war, such as heavyweight ambassador to Washington, anti-corruption reforms, sea-drone strikes on Russia’s shadow fleet, and a clear plan by Zelensky to end the war.“It is time to purge the greedy Servant of the People loyalists feeding off the military budget and to hold accountable those responsible for the shortage of defenses against enemy missiles and drones. sources.headline: Poland reportedly suspends major arms shipment to Ukraine over regional tribute to Ukrainian Insurgent Army, whose fighters took part in WWII massacres of Poles
sources.text: Poland has suspended delivery of a large weapons package to Ukraine over the Lviv Regional Council’s decision to declare 2027 the year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a source told the news outlet RBC Ukraine.Lviv Regional Council members voted at an October 20 plenary session to declare 2027 the year of the UPA, its commander Roman Shukhevych, and Ukrainian political figure Oleh Olzhych.The source told RBC Ukraine that the Lviv regional authorities had “managed” to hold the vote just as Poland was preparing to send Ukraine a large military aid package. “Their irresponsible actions have now put delivery of this package on hold. Intensive efforts are underway through back channels to resolve a problem that was created out of nothing,” the source said.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the Lviv Regional Council’s decision “unwise” and said it “harms Ukraine itself.” Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the decision unacceptable, saying it “deepens divisions” between the two peoples. “The Ukrainian authorities must distance themselves from this position,” he said.Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said Ukraine had assured Poland that the Lviv Regional Council’s decision would not take effect. He said the resolution had disappeared from the council’s website after Poland intervened.The Lviv Regional Council’s Facebook post announcing the year of the UPA is now unavailable.Issues surrounding the Ukrainian Insurgent Army regularly strain relations between Poland and Ukraine. The most recent such dispute arose in the spring of 2026, when Volodymyr Zelensky signed a decree awarding the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA” to the Separate Special Operations Center North, part of the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ Special Operations Forces. The decision drew sharp criticism in Poland because UPA fighters took part in the Volhynia massacres of 1943–1944, in which an estimated 30,000 to 60,000 Poles and 20,000 to 30,000 Ukrainians were killed. sources.headline: Vance defends Trump envoy’s ‘humanitarian’ praise for Putin
sources.text: U.S. Vice President JD Vance backed President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff, who called Vladimir Putin a “humanist.”After meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg, Witkoff thanked the Russian president for releasing U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was convicted in Russia of serving as a mercenary. Witkoff said: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you, and I thank you again.”American journalists later asked Vance whether he agreed with Witkoff’s remarks.I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage. Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said and about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family.Vance said Americans “should all be celebrating” Hubbard’s return, “not be complaining about what [he] said in order to get it done.”Witkoff and Putin met the day after Witkoff held talks with Volodymyr Zelensky and representatives of European countries in Oslo. Witkoff brought new Ukrainian and European proposals for ending the war to the meeting in Russia.After the meeting, the Kremlin said it was ready to resume trilateral talks with the United States and Ukraine between November 10 and 19 (after the U.S. midterm elections). sources.headline: The Kremlin wants Russian media to call attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ‘Putin strikes.’ The inspiration? Stalin.
sources.text: Russia’s Presidential Administration has ordered state and Kremlin-aligned media outlets to begin writing about “Putin strikes” on Ukraine, two employees at such outlets told Meduza.The Presidential Administration’s political bloc sent loyalist media recommendations advising them to report that “the effectiveness and efficiency of Russia’s strikes far exceed what the Ukrainian military has achieved.”“Our ballistic weapons have performed flawlessly. The Ukrainian regime has lost its most important production and storage sites, where cruise missiles and drones, along with their components, were assembled and stored. ‘Putin strikes’ are far larger in scale and more effective than enemy attacks. We are shutting down the militants’ missile programs, which helps keep Russia’s regions secure,” the guidance document says.Headlines, comments from servicemen, and articles using the phrase “Putin strikes” indeed appeared this week in major Russian media outlets.For example, the Russian news website Gazeta.ru published an article with the following subheadline:“SVO” veteran Konovalov: “Putin strikes” deprive the Ukrainian military of the ability to fight.The outlet cites Vitaly Konovalov, head of the Association of Veterans of the Russia-Ukraine War in Stavropol Krai, who says the strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure are allegedly aimed at undermining supplies to the Ukrainian military. Notably, Konovalov himself never uses the phrase “Putin strikes.” It appears in the connecting phrases and generalizations added by propagandists.Novye Izvestia published an article titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Left Without Electricity and Weapons.” Rosbalt used the phrase in the headline of a news item titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Losing Logistics Hubs, Substations, and Vessels.” It also appears in headlines and articles from Fedpress. Segodnia.ru writes about a “series of “Putin strikes.”” The phrase has even appeared in pro-government Instagram accounts.A political consultant who works with the Presidential Administration’s political bloc said directly linking Putin to the strikes on Ukraine is meant to try to boost the president’s approval ratings.According to polls by the Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), Putin’s approval rating fell from 75% in July to 71% in early October, while trust in him fell from 74% to 70% over the same period.“In this case, [the idea is to raise the ratings] among the pro-war, ultra-patriotic segment of society, who need to be shown some successes from the war. To the question “What has been accomplished?” [at the front], the suggested answer is “Putin strikes,” by analogy with the “Stalinist strikes,”” the consultant said.During Joseph Stalin’s rule, the term “Ten Stalinist Strikes” referred to 10 major Soviet army operations during World War II.The source told Meduza that it is hard to assess how effective the appearance of “Putin strikes” in the press has been: “Maybe it will have some effect on the older segment [of society].”Speaking at a press conference in Bishkek on September 1, following the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, Vladimir Putin said he had ordered the Russian military to prepare and carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. “They’re striking our people, so they’ll get a response,” he added.In mid-October, discussing the Russian army’s strikes on Ukraine, Putin said:They took the first step.
